archetype.name: Pocket Passer (vertical)
archetype.definition: A rhythm thrower from the pocket who wins with accuracy and timing at the intermediate and deep levels rather than his legs, and who this year is pushing the ball downfield far more often without giving it away.

report.headline: Throwing deeper and cleaner than ever, but third downs and sacks still cap him
report.take:
Stroud has always been a pocket quarterback first. His legs are a footnote, with 18 carries and mostly short scrambles. His value lives in the intermediate and deep throws, and through seven games those throws are carrying the offense. His 0.468 EPA on throws of 10+ air yards dwarfs the 0.103 he gets underneath. Throws behind the line have cost him -12.4 EPA on their own, so the screen game is a drain the scheme keeps feeding him. The production is real, too. He is 7th in passing yards per game, and his 8.15 adjusted net yards per dropback sits 1.25 over the league average.

The biggest change from last season is how he is throwing, not just how much. His aggressiveness rate jumped to 19.84 from 12.8. You would expect more bad balls from that. Instead his bad-throw rate fell to 11.3 from 16.8, and every season of his career sat well above that. His CPOE is up as well, and he has one interception. Throwing into tighter windows more often while missing less is the profile of a quarterback seeing it better. It does not look like one being reckless. The recent stretch backs that up: 0.242 EPA per dropback over the last three games against 0.119 for the season, with the sack rate cut to 3.0.

The 2-5 record hides more than it reveals. Houston's defense is 24th in EPA and dead last in explosive passes allowed, and two losses were 36-31 and 34-30 shootouts in which he moved the ball. The two genuinely bad games were the week-2 loss to Cincinnati (-6.4 EPA on 55 attempts) and the week-7 loss to the Giants as a 10-point favorite (-0.4 EPA, -9.1 CPOE). The real drag shows up in the situational splits. On third down he averages 8.5 yards to go, a symptom of a run game ranked 25th. He has posted -0.063 EPA there and taken 8 of his 15 sacks there. That 31.1% pressure-to-sack rate is a habit, matching 2023 and 2024. Last year's lower mark looks like the outlier.

Where it heads depends on whether the cleaner accuracy holds. The one-interception line will not: his career interception counts say a few more are coming. The deep-ball efficiency on 36 attempts is also a hot sample, and it should cool toward very good rather than spectacular. The core of it looks durable: fewer bad throws, a willingness to attack, and a top-7 yardage role. With Noel's toe and Montgomery's groin muddying the supporting cast, the next few weeks test how much of it is him.

strengths.title: Attacking downfield without the misses
strengths.body: His aggressiveness is way up on last season, yet his bad-throw rate is the lowest of his career by a wide margin. That pairing is rare. It points to better processing and placement, not just a schematic shift toward deeper calls. Because the bad-throw improvement is so large and runs against his whole career, some regression is likely. Even a partial hold keeps him a top-third passer.

strengths.title: Intermediate and deep throws drive everything
strengths.body: Throws of 10+ air yards produce 0.468 EPA per attempt and account for the bulk of his passing value. Deep balls (0.537 EPA) and intermediate throws (0.425) are both well above anything he gets short. The middle of the field, where he has posted 0.433 EPA, is where he does his best work. The skill is real. The 36-attempt deep sample is the part most likely to cool.

strengths.title: Ball security through the air
strengths.body: One interception in 247 attempts puts his interception rate 1.8 points under the league average. That is remarkable given how much more he is pushing the ball. It partly reflects the cleaner accuracy. It is also partly fortune, since his career interception rankings were middling to poor. Expect interceptions to come back toward normal, though not to his 2024 level.

concerns.title: Third-and-long sack trap
concerns.body: Houston's weak run game leaves him facing long third downs. There he has been below average in EPA and taken more than half his sacks. His pressure-to-sack rate ranks 25th of 38, in line with his first two seasons. This is a trait, not a blip: he holds the ball looking for the downfield answer. That trait pays off on early downs and costs him when the sticks are far away.

concerns.title: Thinning supporting cast
concerns.body: Jaylin Noel was seen in a walking boot after week 7 and is listed questionable. He is Stroud's most efficient target per play at 0.804 EPA. Meanwhile Xavier Hutchinson has drawn the second-most targets at negative EPA per target. David Montgomery is also out, which leaves a run game already ranked 25th with less to lean on. Fewer good options plus worse down-and-distance is how a passer's efficiency erodes.

concerns.title: Red-zone efficiency lags the TDs
concerns.body: Ten touchdowns in the red zone looks great. But his EPA there is barely above zero, dragged down by 4 sacks inside the 20. The touchdowns are real. The process inside the 20 is closer to average, so his touchdown rate should hover near the league norm rather than climb.

trend.note: He opened with two negative-EPA games in three. He then strung together his best stretch in weeks 4-6 (15.2, 10.5 and 13.9 EPA) with minimal sacks. Week 7's flat outing against the Giants is the warning sign, but the last-three and last-five rates are still well above his season marks.

nextGame.headline: Post-bye trip to a stingy pass defense with a soft deep middle
nextGame.body:
The Chargers rank 7th in pass EPA allowed and 9th against short throws. They are also 5th in hit rate, which leans on Stroud's worst habit: absorbing contact and sacks when the first read is not there. Their offense is the worst in the league and the most run-heavy, so this projects as a slow, low-possession game that caps his volume. The opening is downfield. Los Angeles ranks 24th in deep EPA allowed, and that is exactly where Stroud has been at his best. Opponents' second receivers have also run well over their averages against them.

Availability cuts both ways. Derwin James, a 94%-snap safety, and corner Donte Jackson were listed questionable with hamstrings in reports dated before Houston's bye. James playing would tighten the deep middle Stroud wants to attack. On Houston's side, Noel's toe (walking boot, questionable) and Montgomery's absence matter most. Losing Noel removes his most efficient short-to-intermediate target. Losing Montgomery makes early downs harder and third downs longer. Houston has 14 days of rest, which helps Noel's chances.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots versus a soft back end
keyMatchups.body: The Chargers give up 0.712 EPA on deep throws, among the league's worst. Stroud is producing 0.537 EPA per deep attempt. If James is limited, this is where Houston can steal chunk plays in a low-possession game.

keyMatchups.title: Hits and the hold-the-ball habit
keyMatchups.body: Los Angeles ranks 5th in hit rate even though its sack rate is middling. Stroud converts pressure into sacks at a bottom-third rate. On long third downs, this is the matchup most likely to stall drives.

keyMatchups.title: Game script shrinks volume
keyMatchups.body: The Chargers pass less than any team relative to expectation, and their offense ranks 32nd in EPA. That points to fewer Houston possessions and possibly a lead to protect, both of which cut Stroud's attempts. LAC has also held quarterbacks to the 7th-fewest PPR points.

nextGame.watch: Whether Noel plays, and how often Stroud's third downs are long: short third downs keep his sack problem in check against a defense that lives on hits.

restOfSeason.body:
The volume role is secure. He is a top-7 yardage passer on a team whose defense keeps games open, so expect roughly 235-275 passing yards a game, with dips in low-possession matchups like this one. The efficiency gains in accuracy and aggressiveness have enough support across weeks 4-6 to believe in partially. The deep-ball rate and near-zero interception rate are the two numbers set to slide. Something like 0.3-0.6 interceptions a game is more in line with who he has been.

Touchdowns should settle around 1.4-1.9 a game, since his red-zone process is average even though the results have been good. The pressure-to-sack issue is not going away. It is three seasons deep and gets worse when the run game puts him in third-and-long. The swing is the supporting cast: a healthy Noel and Collins keep the efficiency near his recent levels, while a Hutchinson-heavy target tree drags it back toward his season line.
swingFactors: Jaylin Noel's toe and how much of the target load falls to Hutchinson
Run-game health with Montgomery out, and the third-down distances that follow
Whether the drop in bad throws holds as defenses adjust

confidence.note: Seven games with a big accuracy change; deep sample is 36 attempts; key teammates banged up.
